title: API Versioning
subtitle: Evolving APIs safely without breaking mobile and third-party clients via URI paths, headers, and date-based pinning.
keyTakeaways: Mobile apps cannot be forced to update immediately; production APIs must support older versions concurrently for months or years.
URI path versioning (`/v1/users`) is the most common and transparent strategy; date-based version pinning (Stripe model) offers the cleanest client experience.
Deprecation requires active enforcement: use standard `Sunset` and `Deprecation` HTTP headers and monitor telemetry to identify callers still invoking legacy endpoints.
architectureDiagram:
API VERSIONING PATTERNS
1. URI PATH VERSIONING (Explicit & CDN-Friendly)
   GET /api/v1/payments/pay_123
   GET /api/v2/payments/pay_123

2. HEADER / DATE-BASED VERSIONING (Stripe Model)
   GET /api/payments/pay_123
   Header: Stripe-Version: 2026-10-03
   (API Gateway transforms internal response using backward-compatibility middleware)

sections.heading: Comparing the Core API Versioning Strategies
sections.body: Once an API is adopted by external developers or native mobile applications, breaking changes cannot simply be deployed in place. Mobile users may not update their app for months. Engineering teams employ three main strategies to evolve contracts while protecting existing clients.
bullets: URI Path Versioning (`/v1/orders`): The version is embedded directly in the path. Simple for developers to understand and easy for CDNs to cache; downside is potential URI bloat and code duplication across controllers.

Header / Accept Versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json`): Keeps URIs clean and permanent, but makes exploratory testing harder with `curl` or in browsers, and requires configuring CDNs to include the `Accept` header in their cache key (`Vary: Accept`).

Date-Based Version Pinning (The Stripe Model): Clients are permanently pinned to the API date when they created their account. The gateway executes bidirectional request/response transformations on top of a single modern internal codebase.

sections.heading: Deprecation Lifecycles and Avoiding Version Sprawl
sections.body: Supporting five different API versions simultaneously slows down engineering velocity and clutters codebases with legacy conditional branches. A mature API program enforces a formal deprecation schedule backed by observability.
bullets: Telemetry on Callers: Log client user-agents, API keys, and account IDs hitting deprecated endpoints; never guess whether a version is still in use.
Proactive Outreach: Email accounts with active traffic on legacy versions 90, 60, and 30 days before sunset.

Brownout Testing: Intentionally inject intermittent HTTP 410 Gone responses for 15-minute windows during non-peak hours weeks before the sunset deadline to identify forgotten cron jobs before permanent teardown.

tradeOffs.pros: Obvious to developers; works seamlessly in web browsers and Postman; CDN edge caching is trivial without header variance.
tradeOffs.cons: Can lead to duplicated controller code; encourages bumping entire API versions for changes to a single endpoint.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Public developer platforms, mobile app backends, and microservice boundary contracts.

tradeOffs.pros: Single codebase internally; changes are isolated to request/response schema transformer layers; ideal developer experience.
tradeOffs.cons: High engineering investment to build and maintain the bidirectional mutation pipeline.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Enterprise developer-first SaaS platforms with thousands of mission-critical third-party integrations.

interviewTip: When asked how to handle a breaking API change, emphasize backward compatibility first: 'Whenever possible, avoid bumping versions by adding optional fields rather than removing or renaming existing fields. If a breaking change is mandatory, introduce `/v2` alongside `/v1`, emit standard `Sunset` HTTP headers, and monitor API-key-level telemetry to track migration progress.'
